AI-generated plots can speed prototyping and produce code snippets or alternative encodings quickly, but need careful human validation for axis scales, outliers, labeling and reproducibility. Personal example: for a class project on attendance vs. grades I used GPT-4 to generate seaborn plots and a regression fit, which saved hours, but it mis-scaled the y-axis and hid skewed outliers—I manually applied a log transform, switched to robust regression, corrected labels, and documented the fixes.

Quick, iterative visual checks guiding every modeling decision. exploratory plots to find nonlinearity, outliers, and multicollinearity; color and size to encode classes and weights; interactive brushing to test hypotheses on subsets; careful axis scales and colorblind-friendly palettes to avoid misleading impressions. concrete example: for a class project predicting final exam score from a survey of ~500 students and 12 features I made a scatterplot of weekly study hours vs final grade, colored by major and sized by attendance; spotted a tight cluster of about 12 students with high study hours but low scores, investigated and found they had missed the final (a separate flag in the raw log); after flagging those as special-case entries and adding a binary feature for missed-final, model RMSE fell from ~8.3 to ~6.1 and residuals looked more homogenous. visualization as a thinking tool, communication device, and debugging method; always check what a plot might be hiding as well as what it reveals.

Analyzed a dataset of 150 students from my intro data science course; target = final exam score. Cleaned by dropping 10 rows with no score and imputing missing study_hours with the median. Exploratory plots showed study_hours and number_of_practice_problems most correlated with score (r ≈ 0.65 and 0.58). Feature assignment choices: study_hours scaled as continuous, attendance_rate as percentage, prior_GPA continuous, sleep_hours binned into low/medium/high, major converted to STEM vs non‑STEM binary, completed_homework as binary, created interaction term study_hours × practice_problems. Trained linear regression and random forest; encoding and scaling tweaks reduced RMSE from 12.3 to 9.8. Permutation importance and coefficients confirmed study_hours and practice_problems as top predictors. Lesson: targeted EDA plus thoughtful feature assignment (encoding, binning, interactions) materially improved model performance and interpretability.

Data visualization and pattern discovery. Personal example: in a campus bike-share analysis I made hour-by-day heatmaps and geospatial start-point plots that revealed a strong weekday morning peak at 8 AM, a smaller evening commute spike, an unexpected midday lull on Fridays, and a dense cluster of starts by the library during exam weeks; overlaying weather data explained a large dip during a snowstorm that otherwise looked like noise and led me to add weather and calendar features, improving model performance.

For a class project I collected weekly features for 120 students — hours studied, sleep, caffeine intake, lecture attendance, assignment average, practice problems solved, and exam score. Attribute relationships: hours studied and practice problems strongly positively correlated; hours studied negatively correlated with sleep; attendance seemed to mediate the hours→exam relationship, with an interaction where high attendance amplified the benefit of extra study; multicollinearity among hours, practice problems, and assignment average made regression coefficients unstable. I ran PCA on the predictors and got two components explaining 78% of the variance: PC1 loading on hours, practice problems, attendance (an effort axis), PC2 loading on sleep and caffeine (a well‑being/stress axis); using PCs as predictors improved prediction R², reduced multicollinearity, and made clusters and outliers in the student behaviors much clearer.

Used an LLM to brainstorm features and generate preprocessing code for my class project predicting course dropout, accepted several suggestions, but checked its reasoning by implementing the code and then running correlation checks and a logistic model; the model performed worse until I realized the AI had suggested a synthetic "mentorship score" that didn't exist in the raw data and had ignored the confounding between attendance and assignment completion, so I added interaction terms and a simple causal check; takeaway: AI useful for idea and code generation, but its chain of reasoning can skip or invent steps, so always verify each recommendation with data and small experiments.

In my final project predicting exam scores I worked with numeric study_hours and exam_score, categorical major and year, datetime LMS_login timestamps, free-text survey_comments and boolean attended_review. Collected CSVs from the LMS and a Google Form, parsed dates and trimmed whitespace with pandas, dropped duplicate rows, filled missing study_hours with the median and missing attendance with False, one-hot encoded majors, scaled numeric features, merged on student_id with the gradebook, saved a reproducible ETL script with unit tests and Git version control. Explored the cleaned data with histograms of study_hours, scatter plots of study_hours versus final_score with a fitted line, boxplots of scores by major, a daily login time-series, a correlation heatmap, and built an interactive Streamlit dashboard with filters and a colorblind-friendly palette to share findings with instructors.

In my data-mining class I built a classifier to detect fraudulent credit-card transactions. Raw dataset had ~120 features after one-hot encoding, heavy sparsity. I applied PCA as dimensionality reduction to cut to 20 components capturing ~90% variance, and used t-SNE on those components for visualization to spot clusters and mislabeled cases. Trained XGBoost on reduced features; training time dropped ~50%, validation AUC rose from 0.87 to 0.92, and variance between folds decreased (less overfitting). Trade-offs: lost direct feature interpretability, needed to cross-validate number of components, but dimensionality reduction made the classification model faster, more robust, and easier to visualize for stakeholders.

For a customer-churn model I handled messy CRM exports: data cleaning included removing duplicate customer IDs, correcting city-name typos (San Fransisco → San Francisco), parsing signup and last_activity timestamps, stripping dollar signs and commas from revenue, converting types, and imputing missing ages with group medians. Data preprocessing involved engineering tenure from dates, one-hot encoding low-cardinality categories and target-encoding high-cardinality ones, scaling numeric features with RobustScaler, splitting time-ordered train/validation sets, and applying SMOTE to balance the classes before modeling.

Worked on a class project predicting hourly bike-share demand. For preprocessing I parsed timestamps into hour/day/season, engineered lag features and rolling averages, one-hot encoded weather and holiday categories, scaled numeric predictors, removed exact duplicates and clipped trips above the 99th percentile as outliers. For visualization I used time-series plots to spot daily/weekly seasonality, heatmaps of hour vs weekday to guide feature creation, scatterplots and boxplots to inspect relationships and outliers, and a correlation matrix to shortlist predictors. Missing data: temperature had ~6% missing and humidity ~12%; I added missingness indicator flags, applied median imputation for temperature and KNN-imputer for a sensitivity check, compared models trained on imputed vs dropped-row datasets, and found median imputation + missing flag gave the best cross-validated RMSE.

Missing values skewed feature distributions and reduced training set size; I handled them by checking missingness patterns, creating a missing-indicator feature when missingness looked informative, and using median imputation or k-NN imputation when values seemed missing at random. Data inaccuracy produced biased labels and nonsense outliers; I applied range checks, cross-checked suspicious records against source logs, and used robust models and outlier clipping to reduce influence. Concrete example: in a class project predicting final grades I found 15% of homework scores missing and several grade entries like 950 instead of 95 due to data-entry mistakes; I imputed homework with medians for students with similar attendance, flagged and manually corrected obvious typos after verifying raw CSVs, and retrained models with and without corrected records to estimate impact on performance.

Semester project: used deep representation learning with a pretrained ResNet-50 neural network to extract embeddings from 2,400 smartphone images of tomato leaves, fine-tuned top layers on 800 labeled examples, deployed as an AI-powered Flask app; embeddings plus a small classifier raised accuracy from ~68% to ~91%, Grad-CAM showed where the model looked and helped fix mislabeled data, concrete proof learned representations speed up training and make neural-network-based AI more robust in low-data, real-world settings.

Choice of similarity measure driven by data type and task, sensitivity to scale and outliers matters, sparse high-dimensional text behaves differently than dense numeric features, binary/categorical features often need different comparisons, normalization and feature weighting can change results more than the measure itself, metric properties affect which indexing and clustering algorithms are viable, computational cost and need for approximate neighbors matter at scale, threshold tuning and evaluation on labeled pairs or holdout sets required for usable predictions. I used cosine similarity on TF-IDF vectors of student project descriptions to recommend collaborators, normalized and removed stopwords, downweighted overly common terms, set a 0.65 threshold after manual checks, saw false positives from generic phrasing and fixed many by a second-pass Jaccard comparison on extracted keywords, precision improved.

Worked on a city bike-share dataset (≈50k trips): parsed datetimes and computed trip_duration, removed duplicates and impossible durations (<10s or >12h), normalized station IDs and combined rare stations, engineered hour_of_day/day_of_week/is_weekend and estimated trip distance from station coords, log-transformed skewed duration and scaled numeric features before modeling. Missing birth_year and temperature handled with median imputation stratified by user_type and gender for birth_year, KNN imputation (k=5) using hour, station cluster and day_of_week for temperature, added boolean indicators imputed_birth_year and imputed_temperature to keep missingness signal, validated imputation by comparing pre/post distributions and by withholding 5% of observed values to estimate imputation error. Visualized data and checks with histograms and density plots of duration before/after transform, boxplots/violin plots by user_type and gender, scatter of duration vs hour with LOESS trend to show commute peaks, correlation heatmap to spot multicollinearity, missingness matrix to reveal nonrandom gaps, and geospatial scatter of stations sized by trip volume to identify hotspots and guide further feature engineering.

Worked on a campus bike-share demand project where station sensors frequently dropped readings (missing data) whenever the gateway rebooted, and occasional GPS jumps and maintenance logs produced huge spikes (noisy data); data preprocessing: inspected missingness patterns, forward-filled short gaps and used KNN imputation for longer outages, applied median filtering and clipping to remove spikes, created rolling-average features and hour-of-day indicators, normalized numeric features and ensured time-based train/test splits to avoid leakage, which reduced validation RMSE and stopped the model from learning sensor artifacts

Visualization as the first-pass exploration, pattern discovery as the goal. Example from a semester project analyzing city bike-share logs: plotted hourly line charts and weekday-by-hour heatmaps, scatter of trip distance vs duration, and density plots by user type. Visuals immediately showed pronounced morning/evening commuting peaks, shorter average trips on weekends, and a distinct cluster of long-duration leisure rides; also obvious holiday spikes. Those discovered patterns drove feature engineering (time-of-day, weekend flag), targeted outlier handling, and improved the trip-duration prediction model.

Distributed a Google Form to 150 classmates, received 92 complete responses, collected self-reported study hours and sleep hours and exported screen-time CSVs from phone settings for objective phone use, consent via checkbox. Noticed missing values and inconsistent timestamps, cleaned and imputed entries, removed obvious outliers, engineered features like phone-use per awake hour and weekday/weekend flag, one-hot encoded major and normalized numeric features, created binary label for high-study based on a 3-hour threshold. Concerned about sampling bias because respondents skewed toward seniors, class imbalance in the label, used stratified train/test split and cross-validation to check overfitting, monitored feature importance to detect multicollinearity, anonymized IDs and documented data provenance before sharing results.

Visualization choices drove interpretation, using scatter, boxplot, bar chart and time-series to highlight different aspects; data types in my project included numeric ratings, categorical majors and sentiment labels derived from text; concrete example: for my final project I analyzed course evaluations, cleaned comments into positive/neutral/negative, plotted boxplots of numeric ratings by sentiment and bar charts of sentiment counts by instructor plus a line chart of average rating over semesters, which revealed one instructor with declining average and another with high variance, guiding recommendations for follow-up.

Working on a campus study-habits project, about 30% of survey responses lacked major or year information so subgroup comparisons were unreliable; I imputed majors from course lists when clear, excluded ambiguous records for stratified analysis, and documented the reduced effective sample. Self-reported study times contained impossible values (0, 72 hours/day) and mixed units, plus duplicate submissions and typos in free-text study locations, which inflated variance and produced spurious correlations; I cleaned by unit normalization, clipping implausible values, deduplicating, and validating a 10% subsample against time-use diaries, after which the predictive model’s AUC rose from ~0.62 to ~0.76 and subgroup estimates stabilized.

Capstone project predicting hourly bike-share demand, raw CSVs from station sensors and weather API with inconsistent timestamps, duplicate rows, temperature nulls and some sensor spikes. Converted timestamps to datetime and resampled to hourly aggregates, removed duplicates, filtered obvious spikes using IQR thresholds, imputed missing temperatures with median by hour, one-hot encoded weather categories, standardized numeric features, created lag features and rolling averages for demand, dropped near-constant and highly collinear columns after checking correlations, split into train/validation/test, implemented the whole sequence as a sklearn pipeline and saved scalers/encoders for reproducible preprocessing at deployment.

Analyzing three months of my Fitbit step-count data to discover routine patterns: morning commute peaks, lunchtime walks, weekend long hikes, and a steady increase during a running plan. Pattern discovery via clustering of daily 24-hour vectors revealed weekday vs weekend profiles and a small cluster of low-activity sick days. Similarity measures used to operationalize "same pattern": Euclidean distance on normalized hourly vectors for k-means clustering, cosine similarity to match days with similar shapes regardless of overall activity, and dynamic time warping to find similar activity curves when peaks were time-shifted by commuting changes. Preprocessing: imputed short gaps, normalized by daily totals, smoothed with a 3-hour rolling average. Results used to adjust my training schedule and identify days to prioritize rest.

Dimensionality reduction to simplify datasets, reduce noise, speed up training, and make visualization tractable. PCA as my go-to linear technique to compress features before modeling. Personal example: in an accelerometer-based activity recognition project I started with about 120 time- and frequency-domain features, applied PCA and kept 10 components capturing roughly 88% of the variance, classifier training time roughly halved and validation accuracy improved slightly, but component loadings were hard to interpret and some nonlinear patterns were lost. Practical takeaways: scale features before PCA, choose components by cumulative explained variance, and compare against nonlinear methods when needed.

Worked on a news-recommendation project using cosine similarity on TF-IDF vectors to rank related articles, validated recommendations with precision@5; used Jaccard for comparing users' saved tag sets to suggest tag-based matches; switched to Euclidean distance after standardizing numeric metadata (read time, popularity) for k-means clustering of articles; preferred cosine over Euclidean when document length varied to reduce length bias; handled sparse binary features with Jaccard to avoid overstating common absences; inspected nearest neighbors manually and adjusted preprocessing (stopword removal, lemmatization) when mismatches appeared.

In a class project predicting bike-share demand I collected numeric trip counts and durations, categorical weather codes and station IDs, timestamps and GPS coordinates, and short user-type text notes; visualized hourly ridership with line plots and heatmaps (hour vs day), used scatter plots to detect outliers and station-level choropleth maps to show geographic patterns; preprocessing steps: parsed timestamps into hour/day/cyclical sine-cosine features, imputed missing temperatures with hourly medians, one-hot encoded weather and station IDs, log-transformed skewed counts, removed duplicate and erroneous rides, and upsampled low-volume stations for model training.

Worked on a movie-review sentiment classifier: preprocessing included stripping HTML, lowercasing, tokenizing, removing stopwords, lemmatizing, converting to TF-IDF, and balancing classes with SMOTE. Data visualization used word clouds for positive vs negative reviews, histograms of review length, PCA and t-SNE plots of TF-IDF vectors to inspect separability, and confusion matrix / ROC curves to compare models. For classification I trained logistic regression and SVM, tuned hyperparameters with cross-validation, selected the best model by F1 and precision-recall tradeoffs, and iterated preprocessing when visualizations revealed noisy or biased features.

Prefer well-supported libraries like pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, matplotlib/seaborn for EDA and modeling, xgboost/lightgbm for boosting, and MLflow/joblib for experiment tracking and serialization, follow best practices: use isolated environments (conda/venv), Git for version control, modular pipelines and reusable functions, tests for preprocessing and model code, clear docs and config files, notebooks for exploration and scripts or CI for production, ensure reproducibility and data validation, concrete example: for a class project I created a conda env, cleaned data with pandas, built a scikit-learn Pipeline and RandomForest, tracked runs with MLflow, wrote pytest tests for preprocessing functions, committed everything to Git so teammates could reproduce and deploy the model.

Built an AI agent for a class chatbot to answer course logistics; during a live demo it hallucinated and said the final exam was moved to Thursday when no record existed, and a confused student nearly missed the actual date. The hallucination traced back to the agent mixing up imputed schedule fields because the course schedule dataset had missing values for several sessions. I handled missing values by inspecting missingness patterns, using conservative imputation (leave blank or flag as unknown), and adding a provenance layer so the agent cites sources or admits uncertainty. Result: fewer confident but incorrect answers, and clearer handoff to a human when data are incomplete. Key takeaway: agents need missing-data-aware pipelines and explicit uncertainty reporting.

Implemented an RL AI agent to control a simulated delivery robot, lidar point clouds, RGB images, GPS floats and timestamps, categorical terrain labels, scalar battery readings, removed outlier GPS points and interpolated gaps, median-filtered lidar noise, normalized sensor ranges, resized and augmented images, one-hot encoded terrain labels, synchronized and downsampled multimodal streams to 10 Hz, in my capstone I trained that agent on the cleaned data and it reduced collisions and improved route efficiency

AI agents automated labeling and ETL in my capstone pipeline. Concrete example: I had an AI agent extract salary fields from 10k scraped job postings; it often merged adjacent rows when CSVs had stray newlines and hallucinated salary ranges, causing downstream feature leakage. Data verification caught it: random sampling, checksums against raw HTML, schema validation, unit tests for edge cases, and reconciling outputs with original source logs. Tool limitations I hit included context-window truncation, nondeterministic outputs across runs, API rate and file-size limits, brittle scraper connectors, and poor provenance metadata for auditing. Human-in-the-loop review and deterministic rule-based fallbacks proved essential.

Deployed an AI agent to scrape three months of e-commerce product listings; the agent left many price fields null when pages timed out (missing values) and once misparsed a price as 999999 after a locale parsing bug (outlier), so I imputed numeric gaps with category medians, flagged categorical nulls as "missing", clipped extreme values and sent suspicious rows to a human reviewer; takeaway — AI agents accelerate collection but can introduce silent missingness and spurious extremes, so build validation, fallback imputation rules, and human-in-the-loop checks before modeling.

Used an AI agent to automate feature engineering on a course survey dataset, it generated code referencing a non-existent column 'avg_exercise_time' — a hallucination that would have silently introduced errors, caught only because I had the raw CSVs and a data dictionary (data context) to validate column names and sample rows, lesson learned: preserve context and verify agent outputs before using them in analysis.

AI verification: always run sanity checks, unit tests, and spot checks against known aggregates. Incorrect outputs: LLM-generated SQL produced 30% inflated MAU because it used COUNT(user_id) instead of COUNT(DISTINCT) and joined on session_id duplicates, plus it hallucinated a column name and assumed UTC timestamps. Data understanding: inspected schema, nulls, duplicates, timezone, event definitions, and provenance before trusting model output. Personal example: asked an LLM to write a SQL query for monthly active users from our analytics table, rolled it into a pipeline, caught the mismatch during verification when totals didn’t match the dashboard, fixed by checking joins, deduping sessions, adding explicit distinct and timezone conversion. Never push AI-generated code without tests, sample-based verification, and a clear understanding of the data.

AI agents can speed up model deployment but will amplify upstream data issues if not designed for uncertainty, missing values that were never seen during training, and noise in sensors; for example, I built a campus bike‑rebalancing agent that optimized routes using station counts, ran into two full days of missing values from a broken API and highly noisy dock sensors, so the agent started sending trucks to empty stations, we tried median imputation and simple interpolation then added smoothing (Kalman filter) and uncertainty-aware decision thresholds, improvements but still worse when noise spikes coincided with missing blocks, lesson learned: simulate missingness and noise during training, incorporate robust imputations and outlier filtering, monitor agent actions and fall back to conservative heuristics when data quality drops.

In a course project I built an AI agent to form study groups using last semester's sign-up logs, but biased data that overrepresented engineering majors caused the agent to favor homogeneous groups and exclude humanities students, and noisy entries like inconsistent timestamps and missing fields degraded the clustering quality, forcing manual relabeling and a redesign of our data collection process.

AI agents handled large-scale feature extraction and candidate labeling, speeding iteration but amplifying garbage-in-garbage-out when datasets had duplicates, label drift, and missing context. In a summer internship I deployed an automated labeling agent to tag customer support tickets; noisy historical labels and inconsistent text fields caused the agent to propagate errors until we curated a 5k-sample gold set and had subject-matter experts relabel edge cases. Human expertise intervened to define labeling rules, spot sampling bias, and design validation checks; after that the agent's precision rose, model drift reduced, and deployment risk dropped. The takeaway: agents scale work, data quality determines value, and expert judgment is required to close the loop.

In my capstone project predicting final grades from LMS interaction logs, data quality issues were the main hurdle: missing timestamps, duplicated event rows, inconsistent student IDs after roster updates, and bot-generated pageviews that inflated activity. Data preprocessing—standardizing timestamps, deduplicating and reconciling IDs, filtering bots, aggregating session metrics, imputing missing values, encoding categorical variables, and scaling—turned noisy logs into reliable features. After preprocessing, I trained a random forest and a small neural network; AUC improved from about 0.64 to 0.82 and recall for at-risk students increased substantially. AI then enabled earlier identification of struggling students for targeted outreach. Final takeaway: clean, well-preprocessed data amplified model performance; sloppy data produced misleading AI outputs.

Built an AI agent to automatically label microscopy images for an undergrad research project, the agent watched a folder and queued new uploads for inference. Raw TIFF images converted to 8-bit, resized to 224×224, color-normalized per-channel, augmented with rotations and flips, and features vectorized and stored as parquet for training. Verification via a held-out human-labeled test set, confusion matrix thresholds, spot-checking 200 random predictions, unit tests asserting no NaNs and consistent row counts after each transformation, plus input-file hashes to reproduce runs. Result: agent cut manual labeling time by about 60% while maintaining over 90% agreement with expert labels.

As an undergrad working on a course capstone to predict student dropout, I accidentally introduced data leakage by keeping a feature "last_semester_enrollment_flag" that was computed using post-period records, and the model showed suspiciously high accuracy. I had used label encoding on the nominal "major" variable so the model treated majors as ordered integers, which amplified spurious patterns. I relied on an AI agent (GitHub Copilot/ChatGPT) to scaffold the preprocessing pipeline, and its suggested code neither flagged the temporal leakage nor warned against ordinal encoding for that field. After discovering the leak I removed the post-period feature, switched to one-hot encoding, asked the agent to generate time-aware cross-validation code and sanity checks, and ended up with lower but more trustworthy performance and a clearer workflow.

Undergrad project analyzing neighborhood air-quality combining sensor numeric readings, station metadata and citizen comments; mismatched timestamp formats and units broke analyses so I standardized units, aligned timestamps, and imputed gaps to restore data consistency; then I deployed an AI agent to flag anomalous events and generate short summaries for the dashboard, which saved manual review time and improved downstream model performance.

Undergrad project predicting campus bike-share demand. cleaned raw station logs: removed negative counts and duplicate records, imputed missing temperature by linear interpolation from nearest hours, corrected obvious sensor spikes by capping at 99th percentile. used domain knowledge about class schedules and commuting: created features for morning/evening rush based on class start times, marked exam weeks and campus events as high-demand periods, treated weekdays and weekends differently. cyclical encoding for hour of day with sine/cosine, log-transformed the right-skewed rental counts, scaled weather features for models sensitive to magnitude. engineered lag features and rolling averages to capture short-term persistence, ensured train-test splits respected time order to avoid leakage. result: validation MAE dropped substantially once preprocessing reflected real-world campus rhythms rather than blindly applying off-the-shelf cleaning.

AI agents in the pipeline that automate ingestion and model retraining, with decisions grounded in data context — sensor location, calibration logs, time zones, and sampling rates — rather than treating every row the same. preprocessing steps automated by the agent: unit conversion, timestamp alignment, missing-value interpolation, spike detection/removal, seasonal detrending, feature scaling, and encoding of sensor model. concrete personal example: built an agent to monitor three campus weather stations; it used maintenance logs to detect a rain-gauge drift, applied a calibration offset during preprocessing, and cut forecast RMSE from 3.4 to 1.9.

Class project predicting student dropout: data cleaning — removed duplicates, fixed inconsistent course codes, parsed dates, trimmed whitespace, imputed missing GPA with course-level median, dropped rows with no enrollment history. Data preprocessing included one-hot encoding majors and advisors, scaling credits and attendance, creating time-since-last-enrollment, and handling class imbalance by upsampling dropout cases. Noticed bias: dataset overrepresented commuter students and underrepresented low-income, evening students because records came from daytime advising intake, model underpredicted risk for low-income students; compared false negative rates across income groups, reweighted training samples and added socioeconomic proxies to mitigate. Takeaway: cleaning revealed issues, data preprocessing prepared model inputs, but bias persisted unless explicitly tested and corrected.

For a class project predicting course completion I received a dataset with names, emails, grades, timestamps; privacy actions: replaced names and emails with randomized IDs, removed exact birthdates, aggregated small demographic groups to avoid re-identification, stored the raw file on an encrypted drive and shared only the de-identified CSV with teammates, and reported only aggregate metrics in our presentation. For data understanding I performed EDA — histograms and boxplots of grades and time-on-task, a missingness heatmap, timeline plots of activity, correlation matrices, and spot-checked outliers against source records, discovered heavy right-skew in time-spent and label imbalance, and documented data provenance, cleaning steps, and assumptions before modeling.

Built an AI agent in a class project that recommends personalized study plans, reading a CSV export of my gradebook and JSON syllabi from the registrar to get course metadata; data format decisions (CSV for tabular logs, JSON for nested API responses) dictated parsing code, and data types mattered — integers for scores, timestamps for submission dates, categorical course codes, and free-text notes required different preprocessing and feature engineering.

Predicting final exam scores for my stats class project. Initial dataset had many missing homework scores and a few extreme values. I used AI agents to run EDA and propose imputations, which flagged a homework cell of 1000 as an outlier; I checked the raw CSV and corrected it to 100. The AI agents suggested dropping rows with missing homework, but I inspected patterns and found missingness concentrated in a transfer lab section, so I created a missing_homework indicator and imputed medians for the rest. One student had near-zero submissions due to documented medical leave; I kept that row but winsorized the feature for model stability and trained a robust regression. Logged every automated change and kept the original columns to avoid hidden corrections. Human-in-the-loop validation prevented bias from blind AI-driven deletions.

Uncommon data can unlock insights that standard datasets miss, but it carries hidden biases, sensor artifacts, and legal/ethical pitfalls. For my campus project I used Bluetooth beacon logs from a set of Raspberry Pis to estimate pedestrian flow; missing timestamps, randomized MACs, and weekend power outages created gaps, and an early draft of visualizations risked exposing dorm-level patterns so we paused, got IRB guidance, aggregated spatially, removed identifiers, and validated against manual counts. Expect heavy preprocessing, ad hoc feature engineering, and fragile assumptions; validation on external ground truth, clear provenance, and conservative aggregation are essential. Caution with consent, regulation, representativeness, and overfitting; document everything and prefer transparency over flashy but unreproducible claims.

Data analysis: cleaned and aggregated 10,342 campus bike-share trip records, fixed timezone errors and duplicate entries, imputed missing station IDs, built hourly demand heatmap showing morning peak 8–9am and midday lull. AI: trained a random forest to predict next-hour checkouts per station, 85% accuracy on holdout, used predictions to recommend moving two bikes to the five highest-deficit stations. Concrete personal example: last semester I led this April–June project, presented results to campus facilities, they implemented the repositioning plan and morning shortages dropped by about 50%.

Data cleaning focused on reproducibility and auditability: keep raw copies, versioned cleaning scripts, unit tests, and changelogs. In my capstone working with bike-share GPS and weather feeds I resynced timestamps to UTC, removed exact-duplicate trip rows, clipped impossible speeds, imputed short gaps with median speed by hour, and wrote tests that caught a bad timezone conversion before analysis. For AI agents I prototyped an LLM-based agent to propose features and generate EDA code; sandboxed execution, validators, and a human-in-the-loop were necessary because the agent once suggested a join on a nonexistent column. The agent accelerated repetitive coding but required monitoring, logging of decisions, and automated checks to prevent hallucinated transformations.

Choosing data sources — access, licensing, privacy/consent, sampling bias, update frequency, measurement error, metadata and provenance, API limits, cost. For my capstone I combined NYC Open Data restaurant inspection records with Yelp review data pulled via the Yelp Fusion API to predict inspection failures; practical issues I encountered: inconsistent business identifiers requiring fuzzy matching and geocoding, inspections missing outcome fields and dates, reviews biased toward extreme experiences, Yelp API rate limits and terms restricting redistribution, differing update cadences causing temporal misalignment, messy text requiring NLP preprocessing, and the need to document provenance for reproducibility. Resulting workflow: negotiate trade-offs between coverage and legality, heavy cleaning and imputation, feature engineering to align timestamps, and careful reporting of limitations.

Purpose: predict final course grades to identify at-risk students and allocate tutoring resources.  
One concrete project I did: modeled final grades from attendance, homework, and midterm scores, found a clear outlier — a student with zero recorded attendance but a 98 final — investigated with the registrar, learned it was a late-transfer with credits applied, so I flagged the case and ran model sensitivity both with and without that record instead of outright dropping it.  
Outliers: first investigate provenance, correct if data-entry error, otherwise treat as legitimate extreme and consider robust metrics or separate handling; avoid automatic deletion.  
Domain context: institutional policies, grading conventions, transfers and make-up exams change whether an extreme value is meaningful; stakeholder goals (fairness, targeted help) and operational constraints determine how to handle outliers and how to deploy the model.

Built a recommendation agent for campus events that optimized for past click-throughs; failed for incoming freshmen because training logs were dominated by seniors and evening-concerts, temporal and demographic context missing. Realized agent behavior shaped by data context: when, who, device, and event-type distributions in the logs. Fixed by collecting stratified samples, adding features for class year and time-of-day, and testing on a held-out freshman subset. Result: better matches and higher engagement, showing agents only as good as the context represented in their data.

Data understanding: for a house-price project I explored 12k MLS records, histograms of price and area, found heavy right skew in price, many missing year_built values, and high correlation between area and number_of_rooms. Data preprocessing: removed 5 duplicate listings, imputed year_built with neighborhood medians, log-transformed price, one-hot encoded condition, clipped square-footage outliers beyond 3 IQRs, wrapped steps in a scikit-learn pipeline for reproducibility. Verification: unit tests for each preprocessing function, applied pipeline to a holdout set and confirmed no nulls and unchanged row counts, compared summary statistics before/after (mean price within 2%), and spot-checked 20 random rows against the raw CSV to ensure joins and imputations were correct.

For my undergrad project I deployed AI agents to collect, clean, and label my study-session logs from phone usage and Google Calendar. Hypothesized that using the Pomodoro technique (25-minute focused blocks) would lead to higher quiz scores than unstructured study. Data patterns emerged: average quiz scores rose after 1–3 focused blocks, diminishing returns after ~90 minutes, late-night sessions associated with lower retention, short frequent sessions outperformed marathon cramming. AI agents sped up iteration and revealed temporal patterns I wouldn’t have noticed manually.

Senior project analyzing campus bike-share logs: built an interactive dashboard in Tableau and Plotly showing hourly ridership, route heatmap, and weather overlays, which revealed a consistent lunchtime peak and a few stations that needed midday rebalancing. Used an AI agent to draft cleaning scripts, generate SQL aggregation queries, and prototype feature-engineering code — the agent wrote working snippets that I reviewed and adapted, cutting data-prep time from days to hours. Visualization convinced the transportation office to pilot a midday redistribution, the agent sped iteration and reproducibility, takeaway: visuals win stakeholder buy-in, agents automate repetitive work but need human oversight.

Used an AI agent to generate feature-engineering and model-training scripts, requested output as a CSV with columns id, prediction, confidence, concrete example: class project where the agent produced predictions saved to predictions.csv, validation performed by holding out a test set, computing ROC AUC and confusion matrix, and running unit tests to check schema and data types, discovered the agent had swapped id and prediction columns, fixed the output formatting and reran validation before accepting results

During a summer internship I built a demand-forecasting pipeline where an AI agent automated feature engineering and handled null values by mean imputation for many sensor channels. Model accuracy on holdout looked fine, but interpretation tools like SHAP and partial dependence showed flat effects because many entries were imputed at the mean, hiding true nonlinear relationships. After adding missingness indicators and switching to KNN imputation the feature importances changed and the product recommendation reversed, teaching me to treat AI agents' preprocessing decisions as model decisions to inspect rather than trust blindly.

I built an internal Slack ticket-routing AI agent that assigns priority and team based on layered instructions: safety checks first, keyword and regex rules second, ML prediction third, explicit human-override fallback. For training I preprocessed 12,000 historical messages: anonymized PII, removed signatures and quoted text, normalized timestamps, lowercased and removed non-ASCII, corrected common typos, lemmatized, removed stopwords, vectorized with TF-IDF, encoded categorical labels and balanced underrepresented classes with SMOTE, time-based train/validation split to avoid leakage. Clear, testable instructions plus careful preprocessing reduced misroutes and made the agent’s failure modes easier to debug.

Domain knowledge critical when working with medical data; knowing why labs are ordered, typical units, and clinical workflows that create systematic missingness. In a class project predicting 30-day readmission for diabetic patients, HbA1c missing in 40% because primary care only orders it for suspected poor control; clinician explained the pattern, so I added a missingness indicator, used clinic-specific median imputation for baseline models and multiple imputation for sensitivity, and compared model performance and calibration. Missing values often carry signal in medical datasets rather than pure noise; handling them naively biased our coefficients. Privacy constraints and heterogeneous EHR formats forced feature harmonization and limited available predictors. Time stamps, censoring, and treatment effects require feature engineering guided by clinicians.

Worked on a class project predicting final exam scores from LMS activity logs and demographics. Data understanding: examined distributions of time-on-task and assignment grades, discovered heavy right skew in study-time, 12% missing survey responses, strong correlation between midterm and final, imbalance across majors and weekday vs weekend login patterns. Data preprocessing: removed duplicate rows, parsed timestamps into weekday/hour features, imputed missing survey answers with median for numerics and mode for categoricals, log-transformed study-time, clipped extreme outliers, one-hot encoded majors, standardized numeric features, stratified train-test split to preserve pass/fail ratio, implemented the preprocessing steps as a pipeline to prevent leakage.

In a class project analyzing bike-share trip durations I ran into outliers and extreme values when an all-city festival caused many trips to be logged with durations over 48 hours; I used visual plots and timestamp checks, treated obvious logging errors with winsorization after inspection, and kept true long rides that matched user patterns. I used an AI agent (ChatGPT) to generate cleaning code snippets, recommend robust estimators, and suggest diagnostics to distinguish genuine extremes from errors; the agent sped up prototyping but I still verified decisions manually and documented why specific values were removed or retained.

Error detection through automated sanity checks and quick visualizations; spotted anomalies like negative durations and duplicated IDs. Data verification by spot-checking raw files, cross-referencing API logs and provider metadata, and reconciling aggregate counts. Personal example: in a bike-share prediction project I noticed many negative trip durations from a boxplot and summary stats, traced it to a CSV parser misreading timezone and creating swapped start/end times, verified against the original API export and station logs, fixed the parser, deduplicated records, recomputed aggregates, and reran models with improved validation metrics.

Data labeling: annotated 2,000 Amazon review sentences for sentiment (positive/negative/neutral) in an NLP class project, using a short guideline for edge cases and storing labels with timestamps in a spreadsheet. Human verification: a second annotator labeled a random 20% sample, Cohen’s kappa ≈ 0.78, disagreements adjudicated by the instructor and used to refine the guideline. Common issues found: sarcasm, multi-aspect reviews, labeler fatigue on long reviews; relabeled ~150 items after adjudication. Result: verified labels improved cross-validated F1 by about 6 percentage points and reduced systematic bias toward the positive class.

In my capstone project for forecasting building energy, one day's consumption jumped to about 10× the usual and was flagged as an outlier. Initially I treated it as a measurement error and dropped the row; later audit showed a sensor fault caused a negative offset earlier in the month and a calibration reset that day, so removing the point hid an upstream error. I had an AI agent set up to automate cleaning and imputation; it replaced the anomalous day with a smoothed value based on past weeks, which kept model metrics pretty but erased a traceable hardware issue. Lessons learned: don’t let agents auto-correct without provenance logs and human-in-the-loop checks, prefer flagging anomalies for review rather than blind deletion, track pipeline changes so an apparent outlier can point to an underlying error instead of being papered over.

Quick data audit with pandas and visualization of missingness, drop exact duplicates, convert types (strings to datetime), impute area with median and bedrooms with mode, parse date_listed into month and listing_age, one-hot encode neighborhood and label-encode ordinal condition, log-transform skewed area and rent, scale numerics with StandardScaler, detect outliers via IQR and cap at 1st/99th percentiles, remove features with >80% missing or near-zero variance, create new features like area_per_bedroom and age*neighborhood interaction, split data into train/validation/test (70/15/15) stratified by neighborhood, implement all steps in a sklearn ColumnTransformer + Pipeline to avoid leakage, cross-validate and evaluate preprocessing choices, save fitted pipeline with joblib for reproducibility. In a rental-price prediction project with ~10k city listings I applied the above: median imputation for 120 missing area values, one-hot for 45 neighborhoods, log-transformed rent, capped top 1% rents, engineered area_per_bedroom, and used the saved pipeline to preprocess new incoming listings.

In a class project predicting student dropout I practiced AI verification by comparing model outputs to attendance and submission logs and running sanity checks, found a cluster of high-confidence dropout predictions that contradicted strong attendance and traced the issue to data fabrication in the survey (multiple identical free-text answers and impossible timestamps), removed and documented those fabricated records after cross-checking timestamps, duplicate emails, and contacting a few respondents, retrained and recalibrated the model which fixed the bias, and handled sensitive data by stripping names, hashing student IDs, truncating timestamps to the day, storing the dataset on the university's encrypted drive, and only sharing aggregated metrics with teammates.

Missing values in a customer churn dataset I worked on concentrated in income and last-login fields, not missing at random because lower-income customers left more fields blank. I imputed income with the median within ZIP-code clusters, filled categorical occupation with a new "missing" category, and added binary missing indicators so the model could learn patterns in absence. Tried KNNImputer (n_neighbors left at the library default of 5) for a subset and saw little lift over the simple median but much higher runtime. Important gotcha: some libraries and AutoML pipelines silently dropped rows with NA or used SimpleImputer's mean strategy by default, which would have biased income upward in this skewed distribution. Also compared pipelines where XGBoost handled missingness internally vs. explicit imputation — internal handling gave similar AUC but simpler preprocessing. Lesson: check and test defaults, add missing flags, and validate that your chosen imputation doesn't introduce systematic bias.

LLM: rapid generation of code, explanations, and summaries for data tasks; domain-specific use: fine-tuning or retrieval-augmentation for sensitive corpora (medical notes, legal texts, sensor logs) to improve factuality and compliance; AI agents: orchestrate multi-step workflows, call tools (DBs, plotting libraries, validators), and iterate on failures without constant human prompts. Personal example: built an agent around a retrieval-augmented LLM that generated SQL, executed queries on our student-survey database, produced EDA plots, ran basic data-quality checks, and then detected and corrected a mislabeled "satisfaction" column after prompting me for confirmation, cutting turnaround time for the analysis by a large margin.

Built an AI agent to summarize student course feedback and propose prioritized instructor action items. Validation through comparison with three human summaries, blind instructor ratings, and targeted error analysis that exposed hallucinations on niche course jargon. Domain context critical: FERPA-driven privacy redaction, pedagogical norms that reject some automated suggestions, and slang/grade-policy idiosyncrasies that required in-domain fine-tuning. Metrics alone looked good, but human-in-the-loop validation and respect for domain constraints prevented harmful or useless recommendations.

In my capstone I worked with a supposedly de-identified hospital readmission dataset that still included full birthdates and 5-digit ZIP codes. To protect privacy we converted birthdates to year-of-birth, truncated ZIPs to 3-digit, removed names and medical record numbers, applied role-based access for the team, and put a synthetic sample in the public repo. Clinical notes were summarized with an LLM only after stripping identifiers and limiting context, with every AI-generated summary reviewed by a clinician to catch hallucinations or leaked details. The experience showed how sensitive data can be inadvertently exposed and how AI summaries can amplify risks if identifiers or inaccurate inferences slip through; human review and careful preprocessing are non-negotiable.

Course project: asked an LLM to draft methods and results for a sales-data analysis; AI hallucination fabricated a citation (Smith et al., 2019) and invented a mean revenue ($12,345) that didn't match my dataset (actual mean $1,234); almost submitted it; caught the fabrication when I reran the script; now require code-generated numbers for every reported stat, citation verification, and label model prose as draft-only.

Built an AI agent for delivery-route optimization in my junior capstone for a local courier; agent trained to propose and adjust routes in simulation, rather than hand-coding heuristics. Domain knowledge encoded directly into the state and reward: delivery time windows, vehicle capacities, typical rush-hour slowdowns, parking constraints and no-left-turn streets. Data preprocessing was crucial: cleaned noisy GPS traces, imputed missing timestamps, map-matched points to roads, aggregated address-level stops into delivery zones, normalized temporal features, and removed obvious outliers. Result: simulated routes cut average route time by about 12% and surfaced recurring bottleneck streets for the company to address.

AI agents need continuous monitoring because they silently accumulate errors; in my capstone project I deployed a Slack bot agent to recommend campus events that, after an upstream CSV schema change, began recommending past events and unrelated pages — discovered when user complaints rose and error logs showed malformed timestamps, fixed by rolling back the data pipeline, adding schema validation, realtime alerts for metric drift, and a human review step to catch future errors.

Data privacy: when I built a campus housing occupancy predictor using swipe-card logs I stripped names and IDs but initially overlooked unique movement patterns that could re-identify individual RAs, so I switched to daily aggregated counts, minimized retention, and required explicit opt-in for sensitive logs. Human oversight: the model once flagged a low-occupancy weekend and was about to auto-lock common rooms, but a resident advisor reviewed the anomaly and prevented the lockout—reinforced need for human-in-the-loop, manual overrides, and audit trails. AI assumptions: the model assumed fall-term arrival patterns and consistent device usage; orientation week and a shift to remote classes violated those assumptions and caused degraded predictions, so we documented assumptions, ran edge-case tests, and set distribution-shift monitoring.

In my capstone project I deployed an AI agent to auto-label IoT sensor events for a predictive-maintenance model; the agent produced systematic labeling errors after daylight-saving misaligned device timestamps, causing the model to learn time shifts instead of true failure patterns. Caught the problem by plotting event timelines and finding misalignments and impossible negative lead times. Fixed it by adding data validation rules: timestamp consistency checks, duplicate and gap detection, value-range assertions, and a manual review step for edge cases. Lesson learned: AI agents can introduce subtle errors that cascade through pipelines, so proactive validation and small human-in-the-loop checks prevent wasted training and misleading metrics.

Course-performance prediction project using campus records, LMS logs, and prior GPA. Data understanding: EDA showed 20% missing assignment scores, heavily skewed engagement time, and high correlation between prior GPA and final grade, so I imputed missing scores differently by feature and log-transformed engagement. Statistics: ran t-tests to compare section means, used bootstrap to get 95% CIs for accuracy and AUC, checked calibration with Brier score and computed subgroup difference-in-means with p-values. AI verification: temporally split 5-fold cross-validation, calibration plots and isotonic regression, subgroup performance checks for equity, manual inspection of 50 misclassified cases to find label noise and feature edge cases, retrained with corrected labels and noise-aware loss. Result: initial AUC 0.78 overconfident probabilities; after fixes and calibration AUC bootstrap CI 0.75–0.80 and false negatives down 30%.

Human role: framing the question, choosing objectives and evaluation metrics, curating and labeling data, enforcing ethics and fairness, interpreting results and deciding trade‑offs. AI agents: fast copilots for exploration and automation, generating candidate features, code snippets, model ideas, or even running experiments when given clear constraints, but needing human verification and guardrails to catch errors and biases. Prompting: an iterative craft — give concise context, schema, objectives, and constraints; include examples and expected formats; refine based on outputs. Concrete example: in my semester project predicting course dropout I fed the dataset schema and target definition to an AI agent, prompted for feature engineering ideas and SQL queries with a note to avoid time‑leakage, reviewed and tested the suggested features, discarded leaky ones, kept useful transformations, adjusted for fairness, and wrote the final model and evaluation myself.

AI agents can automate and orchestrate repetitive parts of a pipeline and surface uncertain cases for human review; large datasets improve model robustness but increase cost, noise, and bias risk. In a class project I built a simple agent to scrape and label 120,000 product reviews, retrain a sentiment model iteratively, and send low-confidence samples to teammates for relabeling. Result: accuracy rose from ~78% to ~88%, but label noise and class imbalance in the large dataset introduced systematic skew toward neutral predictions and long training cycles that forced me to subsample and adopt incremental training. Tradeoff: agents scale workflows across large datasets but need monitoring, bias audits, and infrastructure planning.

Missing values in a student-performance dataset from a class project: attendance and self-reported study-hours had about 20% missing because some students skipped the week-1 survey. I first applied simple median imputation for study-hours and a forward-fill for recent attendance, plus a missingness indicator column. Model accuracy looked good at first, but human oversight—manual inspection of imputed value distributions and conversations with the course staff—showed missingness concentrated among low-performing students who often skipped the survey, so the naive imputation biased results. I switched to multiple imputation conditioned on past grades and demographics, retained the missingness flag as a feature, compared performance across imputed datasets, and documented why the manual review changed the pipeline; outcome: reduced bias and more trustworthy predictions.

Capstone traffic-simulation project using an AI agent to optimize signal timings, trained in simulation on collected sensor logs. Data preprocessing included syncing timestamps across sensors, removing duplicated records, imputing missing counts from nearby sensors, scaling features, and flagging outliers that broke models. Human oversight through weekly review meetings, manual sanity checks on agent-recommended schedules, and a kill-switch during live tests. Concrete example: I discovered a mislabeled sensor that made the agent favor one lane, fixed the label and re-ran preprocessing, then the agent adopted fairer timings and reduced congestion in the campus simulation. Lessons: preprocessing and human oversight changed agent behavior more than tweaking hyperparameters.

In a semester project predicting student final grades from LMS logs I ran into accuracy issues when mobile-app timestamps were shifted by several hours because of a server timezone bug, which produced implausible session lengths and inflated engagement features; I fixed this by cross-referencing raw server logs and removing sessions that still looked erroneous. Sample bias toward students who regularly used the LMS and consented to data collection produced overrepresentation of engaged, higher-performing students; I reweighted the training set to match registrar demographics and prior-GPA distributions and performed sensitivity analyses to measure how much the bias affected predictions. Many demographic fields and a few assignment scores were missing for transfer students, so I used targeted imputation for low-variance features, added missingness indicators, and dropped records only when key predictors or the outcome were entirely absent. Final model performance improved modestly, but I documented the remaining accuracy problems, residual bias, and the extent of missing-data imputation in the report.

Built an AI agent in a course project to triage campus IT help tickets and suggest routing and priority, trained on past tickets and resolution logs. data types: unstructured ticket text and screenshots, categorical issue labels, numeric response times, timestamps and user metadata. data context: campus-specific jargon, privacy constraints, seasonal exam-period surges, and differences between student and faculty requests affected model inputs and evaluation; incorporating context features (user role, course calendar) improved accuracy and reduced misroutes.

I built an AI agent to triage customer support tickets for my internship; hypothesis: adding a learned priority score and automated first-response drafts would reduce average response time and escalate fewer tickets; data patterns in the logs showed 40% faster responses for high-priority tags, recurring spikes in unanswered tickets around 15:00, and higher escalation rates for messages containing product-error phrases, so I adjusted the agent’s threshold and rerouted afternoon traffic for retesting.

In a class survey I ran on study habits and mood (n=412) missing data were common. A server outage at 2 a.m. randomly dropped about 30 responses — MCAR. Questions about family income were skipped disproportionately by students who reported scholarships and part‑time jobs — MAR. Several participants who initially reported very high depressive symptoms quit before finishing the mood inventory, suggesting MNAR. I handled this by inspecting missingness patterns, using complete‑case only where MCAR seemed plausible, multiple imputation with observed predictors for MAR, and sensitivity checks / pattern‑mixture style reasoning for the suspected MNAR.

LLMs reflect the biases present in their training data; in my course feedback project the model consistently paraphrased nonstandard English into neutral-standard phrasing and downplayed culturally specific concerns from international students, so the output looked more positive than the raw responses. Data understanding mattered: the survey had far fewer responses from international students, no metadata on language background, lots of short comments, and some ambiguous labels — all of which made the model’s summaries unrepresentative. Human interpretation was essential: I sampled raw vs. summarized texts, flagged mismatches, re-labeled a validation set, and presented summaries with caveats rather than as definitive findings, and we used human reviewers to prioritize issues the model missed.

Data format: pick a single canonical schema early, store raw immutable dumps (JSON/ndjson) plus a cleaned tabular CSV with strict types and ISO timestamps, and include a small data dictionary. Extraction: automate API pagination and incremental SQL pulls, version raw extractions, log failures, and build lightweight ETL scripts in Python to flatten nested fields and normalize encodings. AI verification: use a large model to generate sanity-check rules, inspect random samples, flag anomalies, and produce human-readable summaries and test assertions for the pipeline. Personal example: scraped 12,400 product reviews as nested JSON, flattened to a canonical CSV, wrote ETL to normalize multi-valued tags and timezones, then used GPT to scan 200 samples and propose regex checks that caught inconsistent dates and mislabeled ratings, cutting downstream label errors from ~7% to ~1%.

AI agents sped up feature engineering and hypothesis generation in my hospital internship sepsis project.  
Domain expertise from ICU clinicians revealed confounders and clinical interventions the agent missed.  
Data relationships were complex: non-linear, time-lagged, and modulated by treatments.  
Concrete example: the agent flagged rising heart rate as sepsis risk, clinicians pointed out scheduled beta‑blocker weaning caused transient tachycardia, we added a vasopressor/beta‑blocker variable and interaction terms, false positives fell markedly and AUC improved.

AI agents processed thousands of survey responses for a class project, speeding up tokenization and initial labeling but producing repeatable, opaque mistakes; constant human supervision was needed to sample outputs and catch patterns. In my project the agent labeled resumes and job-fit scores, and I found a clear bias: female names were 30% more likely to be scored as "less technical" because the training examples skewed male; I manually audited a subset, corrected labels, and augmented the dataset with balanced examples before retraining. Lesson: never fully trust automated agents, institute human-in-the-loop audits, monitor fairness metrics, and iteratively fix biased patterns.

In my capstone project predicting student exam scores I used an AI agent to propose preprocessing and model pipelines; it suggested mean imputation for missing quiz scores, target encoding for section IDs, and a Random Forest candidate. Verification: ran k‑fold CV and a held‑out test, inspected residuals and feature importances, wrote small unit tests to ensure no data leakage and that imputed values stayed within realistic ranges, and reimplemented the agent’s pipeline in a clean script to reproduce results. Human review: showed the pipeline and diagnostics to my TA and a teammate, who noticed the mean imputation masked a subgroup pattern and the target encoding could leak information across folds; we switched to group‑wise imputation and nested CV, which reduced apparent overfitting. Lesson: AI agents accelerate exploration, but systematic verification and human review catch subtle errors and bias.

On an online sports retailer I typed running shoes and the search suggestions showed running shoes size 10, running shoes insoles, trail running shoes; I clicked the insoles suggestion which saved time, on the product page a frequently-bought-together module recommended insoles, running socks, and shoe cleaner — those recommendations came from association rules mined from past baskets and led me to add insoles and socks to my cart, demonstrating how search suggestions speed up finding the right query and association rules surface complementary items for cross-sell.

In retail I noticed market basket analysis when the store placed salsa next to tortilla chips and sent me a coupon. Last week I personally bought tortilla chips and salsa together, matching the purchasing patterns the retailer used to design that endcap and targeted discount. Concrete impact on product placement, bundling, and cross-sell tactics.

Hobby project analyzing web novels: I treated each user reading session as a basket of tags and applied market-basket analysis to tag co-occurrence; concrete example — on 1,200 sessions from a niche web-novel site I discovered high lift between "slow-burn romance" and "office politics" and between "isekai" and "progression fantasy", so I surfaced tag-based bundles in a sidebar; result: recommendation click-through up ~22% and dwell time on recommended novels +14%.

In a semester project analyzing 1,200 course evaluations I applied NLP to preprocess and vectorize free-text responses, extracted word patterns with regex and n‑grams like "too fast", "not enough examples", "slides unclear", and then ran association rules that showed "too fast" ⇒ "slides unclear" with support 0.12 and confidence 0.68, which directly informed our recommendation to slow pacing and improve slide clarity.

Track game purchases and in-game item co-occurrences, run market basket analysis to surface frequent co-purchases and purchase sequences, use results to design bundles and targeted cross-sells. Personal example: during a Steam sale I bought Hades, then within a week bought the soundtrack and a USB controller — a bundled offer (game + soundtrack + controller discount) would have saved me money and likely increased my immediate spend. Bundle strategy: curated genre bundles, starter packs (game + key DLC + tutorial content), timed bundles for seasonal sales, personalized bundle offers based on a user’s basket history; evaluate by uplift in conversion and average order value, A/B test price points and promotion placement.

Course enrollment in my department skewed toward pairing Data Science 101 with Intro to Python and Statistics. Frequent itemset found {DataScience101, IntroPython, Statistics101} with high support among freshmen. Pattern mining revealed a common sequence: Intro to Python → Data Science 101 → Machine Learning next term. Concrete personal example: I enrolled last semester in Data Science 101, Intro to Python, and Linear Algebra; that same co-enrollment appeared in the frequent itemset for my cohort and pattern mining correctly predicted that several of us would take Machine Learning this term (three of my classmates and I did).

Worked on bot detection in games using pattern mining; instrumented a browser-based multiplayer puzzle game for a class project, logged actions and timestamps from ~1,000 sessions, mined frequent sequential patterns and timing motifs, found a cluster with near-constant inter-click intervals and identical 4-action repeats, inspected session recordings and IPs to confirm automated play, removed those accounts and observed improved match fairness and reduced server spikes; lesson: pattern mining surfaces behavioral signatures but needs human validation and periodic retraining to handle adversarial adaptation and avoid false positives.

At the supermarket, market basket analysis revealed an association rule linking pasta purchases to pasta sauce; I experienced it when I grabbed a box of spaghetti and a jar of marinara on the same trip.

Course registration: when I signed up this semester I and many classmates chose CS101 and Math201 together; out of 200 students 80 took CS101, 60 took Math201, 50 took both. Frequent itemset: {CS101, Math201} appears in 50 registrations (25%). Association rule: CS101 -> Math201 has confidence 50/80 = 62.5% and lift ≈ 2.08, suggesting students who enroll in CS101 are over twice as likely to also enroll in Math201 compared with the baseline.

Analyzed an online store transaction log with market basket analysis; found an association rule {USB-C cable} -> {phone case} (support 0.04, confidence 0.52, lift 1.8); concrete personal example: purchased a new phone from that store and three days later bought a clear case and tempered-glass screen protector, matching the rule; recommended bundling those items and sending targeted cross-sell emails.

On an e-commerce site I added running shoes to my cart and the page immediately suggested performance socks and insoles based on an association rule learned from past transactions (shoes → socks/insoles), the recommendation system surfaced those items on the product page and in a follow-up email so I bought socks too, faster checkout and useful cross-sell.

Movies I watch skew toward thrillers and mysteries, concrete personal example: of 50 films I watched this semester 20 labeled thriller, 18 labeled mystery, 15 were both thriller and mystery — association rule {thriller} => {mystery} with support 15/50 = 0.30 and confidence 15/20 = 0.75, used that rule to build weekend playlists and recommend titles like Prisoners and Zodiac together.

On my e-commerce site for tech accessories, used market basket analysis; found an association rule {USB-C hub} -> {laptop stand} with support 6%, confidence 48%, lift 1.8; created a bundle and a targeted pop-up based on that rule, resulting in a 12% increase in average order value and a 9% lift in bundle conversions.

Online shopping: my viewing history showed pages for trail running shoes, blister-prevention socks, and a GPS watch; frequent itemset suggestions surfaced energy gels and a headlamp; concrete personal example — after viewing those three items I clicked the recommended energy gels and bought them.

On Coupang I bought a silicone phone case and the site's recommendation systems immediately suggested a tempered-glass screen protector and a fast USB‑C charger, a concrete example of market basket analysis at work since customers who buy cases often buy protectors and chargers, seeing those recommendations convinced me to add the charger to my cart, showing how integrating market basket analysis into recommendation systems can increase conversions and inform product bundling and promotion strategies on Coupang.

Studying the campus wetland ecosystem through a semester project, I catalogued biodiversity via smartphone photos and eDNA swabs (about 45 taxa over three months) and applied pattern mining to time-stamped presence/absence and sensor data; one concrete personal example: weekend transects where I uploaded 120 photos to iNaturalist, then used association-rule mining to find a strong co-occurrence between damselflies and emergent macrophytes and a clear shift in species clusters after a heavy rain event, informing hypotheses about habitat preferences and sampling bias.

Supermarket purchasing patterns show clear weekly cycles and promotion-driven spikes, cross-product associations revealing common basket mixes, loyalty-card timestamps useful for mapping shopping journeys and optimizing restocking, heatmaps of aisle traffic informing layout changes. Concrete personal example: I buy coffee beans and bananas every Saturday morning, added a granola bar after seeing an in-aisle sample and a 15% mobile coupon, and started buying a different brand when the store placed it next to the coffee display. Insights like these help forecast demand, tailor targeted discounts, test layout experiments, and reduce stockouts.

At my local supermarket, market basket analysis was obvious when I grabbed pasta and jarred sauce last week; they were on the same endcap, my loyalty app pushed a coupon for garlic bread after checkout, and I ended up buying all three on impulse.

Using watch history as implicit signals to infer topical interests for podcast recommendations, feature engineers pull video transcripts, watch duration, and session context to build user embeddings; temporal decay and device/context (commute vs. evening) weight recent video behavior more heavily; cross-domain transfer helps surface long-form audio when users binge related videos; balance collaborative signals with content embeddings to handle novelty and reduce filter bubbles; privacy controls to clear or pause watch history for user trust. Concrete example: after binge-watching urban planning documentaries on YouTube, the recommender suggested a city-design podcast episode I played on my evening commute and then subscribed to.

Combining aviation operations with travel-pattern analysis to drive smarter marketing: using booking lead times, origin–destination flows, and flight-level utilization to forecast demand and tailor offers that shift passengers onto underfilled flights and sell ancillaries. On a recent trip last December I flew BOS→MCO and got a personalized weekend-family bundle email that I purchased on checkout — concrete proof that timely behavioral segmentation converts. Models I use: clustering by trip purpose and booking cadence, time-series for route demand and delay propagation, uplift tests for promo effectiveness; business outcomes: higher load factors, better yield per flight, improved ROI on ad spend. Must balance targeting with privacy and avoid reinforcing biased service patterns.

Medical records as primary data source, both structured vitals/labs/codes and unstructured clinician notes, messy timestamps and inconsistent symptom phrasing. Symptoms as key predictive features, need extraction, normalization, encoding of severity and timing, and attention to missingness and bias. Personal example: my ER visit for suspected appendicitis — triage note "sharp RLQ pain 12 hrs", fever 38.5°C, WBC 14.2k, CT report confirming inflamed appendix, operative and discharge notes documenting symptom progression. Preprocessing priorities: deidentify, use NLP to pull symptom mentions, create temporal symptom trajectories, engineer severity indicators, validate against imaging/lab results. Ethical and privacy constraints shape what can be used and how models are evaluated.

As a data science undergrad I applied data mining to telemetry from a casual mobile game I helped prototype, finding an association rule: players who used the "double reward" booster in their first three sessions had a 68% probability of making an in‑app purchase within the first week versus 12% for others, so we targeted a starter offer to those users and saw conversion lift in A/B testing

Analyzing movies as data: ratings, genres, release dates, box office, and review text used for recommendations and trend forecasting. Concrete example: used MovieLens 100k to build a simple recommender for roommates — cleaned missing ratings, trained matrix factorization, added genre bias, got RMSE ~0.93 and friends rated recommendations 7/10 useful. Watch out for popularity and recency biases, sparse ratings for niche and foreign films, and ethical choices around personalization that can create filter bubbles.

Illnesses rarely occur in isolation, co-occurrence influences diagnosis, treatment plans, and outcomes. Pattern mining on EHRs and claims can surface recurring illness combinations and temporal sequences that flag likely complications or screening needs. Personal example: last winter I caught influenza A and five days later developed a bacterial sinus infection that required antibiotics. Practical challenges include noisy coding, temporal ambiguity, confounding by medications or age, and class imbalance. When applied carefully, pattern mining helps prioritize prevention, tailor follow‑up, and allocate clinical resources.

KPOP merchandise analysis using market basket analysis revealed a strong association rule: purchases of a BTS album often imply purchase of an official lightstick; personal example: last month I checked out on the online store with a BTS album, added the official lightstick and a photocards pack in the same transaction; in our store data the rule {album} -> {lightstick} had ~4% support and ~62% confidence, suggesting a bundle promotion and targeted cross-sell at checkout.

On my last dozen food delivery orders I always add a side of fries when I order a burger; a quick market basket analysis of my past orders produced the association rule {burger} -> {fries} with high confidence, the delivery app now surfaces fries as a suggested add‑on and I click it more often, increasing my average order value and speeding checkout.

Netflix uses my viewing history to make recommendations, concrete personal example: after I binge-watched Stranger Things and Black Mirror Netflix recommended Dark and I watched it, association rule learned from my history: {watched Stranger Things, watched Black Mirror} -> {watch Dark}

On my music streaming account (Spotify) I compared my "Gym" and "Running" playlists; frequent itemset analysis found "Blinding Lights" and "Don't Start Now" as common songs, so I auto-generated a high-tempo workout playlist from that intersection

Summer internship at a hospital: web log analysis of the patient portal (10,452 sessions over 6 months). Association-rule mining revealed {chest-pain symptom page, medication-history page} -> {schedule cardiology appointment} with support 3.8% and confidence 68%. Implemented an inline prompt and fast-track triage based on that rule, resulting in a 22% increase in same-month cardiology referrals and earlier diagnoses of arrhythmia in several patients.

Ran market basket analysis on my last 120 food delivery orders and found an association rule: pad thai → spring rolls (support 0.15, confidence 0.72, lift 1.6). One night I ordered pad thai, the app suggested spring rolls based on that rule, I accepted the bundle, and my average order size increased — concrete example of using association rules to drive food delivery recommendations.
